newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed's Moskow says inflation progress made.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed's Moskow says inflation progress made.

text.p: Chicago Federal Reserve President Michael Moskow said considerable progress has been made toward reducing U.S. inflation but price stability has not yet been achieved.
"I think we've made a lot of progress on achieving a low rate of inflation, although we're not yet at price stability," Moskow said in the text of a speech released here for delivery in California.
Moskow also said the United States needs to boost domestic savings to increase productivity.

He said the U.S. has been "dodging bullets for years" because of investment flows into the U.S. from overseas, but said that ultimately, the level of investment in an economy is determined by domestic savings.
"We need to increase domestic savings to increase productivity," he said. "The best way to increase domestic savings is to reduce the federal budget deficit."

He noted some progress on the U.S. budget deficit in recent years, saying the deficit last year it was just under 1.5 percent of gross domestic product, the smallest percentage since 1974. In 1992 the deficit was five percent of GDP.
"So although we've made some progress, we shouldn't be too comfortable yet," Moskow said. Reducing the federal budget deficit was a key item on Moskow's "wish list" for the 21st century.
At this stage in the U.S. economic expansion, "ideally, we should be running a surplus," he said.

Moskow also said he was surprised at the level of insecurity among U.S. workers, given the relatively low current unemployment rate of around 5.25 percent. He said demand for labor has been quite strong and wages rose faster in 1996 than in 1995.

But he said worker displacement rates, although lower than they were in the 1980s, are still high considering the low unemployment rate. And, he said, displacement has spread more evenly throughout the economy.
"These changes seem to have created deep feelings of job insecurity," Moskow said.
"It seems the insecurity in the work force has helped to hold down wage pressures. Workers apparently have been willing to trade off higher wage increases in exchange for enhanced security," he said.
